item.title: How GTA VI Became the Most Expensive Video Game Ever Made
item.description:
It took over a decade to make Grand Theft Auto VI. And when it's released on November 19, it will have already set at least one record: the most expensive video game ever made. In the years since the last GTA release, the video game industry has changed massively. Investors, once excited by the prospect of blockbuster video games, have pulled back, sales have stagnated, and the industry as a whole seems more precarious. Bloomberg News video game reporter Jason Schreier has been following Rockstar Games and its quest to release GTA VI for a long time. Ahead of the launch, we speak with him about why it took 13 years — and a budget that reportedly exceeded $1 billion — to get GTA VI across the finish line, and his impressions of the game having played it before almost anyone else on the planet. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Trump, Xi Hug Ahead of Unprecedented Talks with Russia’s Putin
item.description:
In a rare move, Chinese President Xi Jinping greeted US President Donald Trump with a hug on arrival in Shenzhen, ahead of an unprecedented trilateral meeting between the two leaders and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Before Trump’s arrival, Xi warned against economic barriers and urged closer cooperation among Asia-Pacific nations, as new US restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips strain a fragile trade truce. Nvidia sought to deliver a clear message during its first earnings update since the departure of longtime leader Jensen Huang. The chip giant boosted its sales forecast for next year and vowed to improve Nvidia’s access to critical supplies, while tamping down speculation that Huang might return. Today’s guests: Michael Strobaek, Lombard Odier Global Chief Investment Officer; Melanie Garson, University College London Associate Professor; David Kirtley, Helion Energy Founder & CEO (Source: Bloomberg)

Deutsche Bank’s stock dropped on reports that it processed $582 million of suspicious payments linked to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and sought to expand its Russian business before the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. The firm and some of its backers seeking to raise as much as $90.4 billion in the share sale and a separate private placement. item.title: The Impossible Trilemma Hanging Over the Nvidia Crisis
item.description:
Tian Yang, CIO and manager of the VPX fund at Variant Perception, recently published a report called “The Sovereign Impossible Trinity” that is especially salient right now. Yang's thesis is that the US-China rivalry is exposing three main policy trade-offs: The necessity of sovereignty (which both of the great powers insist on) means that neither state can assure they can maintain the trio of guns (or the AI 'arms race'), butter (social spending), and sound money because of physical constraints, political conditions, and inflation. Given that the US-China AI arms race forms the backdrop of the upheaval at Nvidia, you can't understand Jensen Huang's resignation without considering geopolitical and global economic conditions. Yang talks to us today about why Jensen might be our era's Oppenheimer and what it means that the biggest powers in the world can't maintain sound monetary policy while also upholding defense and entitlements. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Why a $2 Billion Law Firm Suddenly Collapsed
item.description:
At the end of October, seemingly overnight, a major law firm called Weil Gotshal announced it was winding down after a number of partners departed and talks of a merger with another firm failed. So how did a $2 billion big law firm collapse in the span of a few weeks? In 2015, Yale Law professor John Morley published a paper called "Why Law Firms Collapse," that now looks very prescient, with his idea of a “partner run," or the law firm version of a bank run. What is especially interesting about Morley's paper is his forensic examination of partner-led businesses and the idea that the model might be inherently fragile. In this episode, we talk to Morley about his newly relevant paper, the collapse of Weil Gotshal, whether AI will really change how law firms are run, and the future of big law. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: The Perfect Storm That Clobbered Hedge Funds
item.description:
Even before the midterms, the AI trade was weakening. Just look at all the headlines from October in the hedge fund world — it was one of the bloodiest periods the industry has faced in recent memory. Now, after the blue wave, things continue to look uncertain. So what's going to happen with the AI buildout now? And what about the big Anthropic IPO? Today's episode is a two-parter, one that examines both the hedge fund carnage of the last few weeks and the broader macro conditions we find ourselves in after the midterm elections. We speak with two of our Bloomberg News colleagues — Nishant Kumar, chief correspondent for hedge funds, and macro strategist Michael Ball — and they help lay out why October was a historic month for hedge funds and what they are paying attention to now as jitters from the AI trade continue to work their way through the market. Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Berlin, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. Global stocks climbed as investor enthusiasm for the artificial intelligence trade outweighed concern that hotter-than-expected US inflation will prompt the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates further. CoreWeave eased fears about its debt-laden business during a high-stakes quarterly report, indicating that sales growth remains strong despite challenges facing the data center industry. Plus, Anthropic’s bankers are weighing plans to increase the company’s valuation in its IPO to $1.5 trillion or more, the Financial Times reported. Today's guest: Christian Bruch, Siemens Energy, CEO. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.author: Min Jeong Lee and Komaki Ito

item.title: This Is How New York City Takes Out Its Trash
item.description:
According to Joshua Goodman, trash collection in New York is one of the last services the city offers that is not yet touched by neoliberalism. What he means is that it's the last free and unlimited city service — there is no opt-in; it is not means tested. Goodman — who is the DSNY's deputy commissioner for public affairs and customer experience — tells us that the city deals with 24 million pounds of trash every day, and on today's podcast, he explains the logistical dance required to sort through all that garbage. We also get into why NYC produces less trash than you might think, the DSNY's new containerization program (and the new side-loading trucks they built in less than 18 months), and why recycling is not a scam. (Source: Bloomberg)

We don't need to tell you that the midterm elections were historic: The Democrats won bigger than even they imagined. But as the dust settles, an open question we are puzzling over is the market's ongoing reaction to this massive political sea change. Democratic control of Congress — and control over a number of formerly red statehouses like Texas and Iowa — will influence everything from the composition of the FOMC to data center construction. And what we're seeing right now, with stocks like Tesla and SpaceX tumbling, is a direct response to these conditions. To get a better sense of this macro moment, we turn to Odd Lots regular, Employ America's executive director Skanda Amarnath to talk about how the midterms will influence the Fed's battle with inflation, Elon Musk's political instincts, and what a Democratic majority means for the market, tariffs, and AI. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Global Tech Selloff Deepens as US Midterms Trigger AI Fears
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Live from Brussels, we set the agenda for your day, catching you up with overnight markets news from the US and Asia. And we'll tell you what matters for investors in Europe, giving you insight before trading begins. The global stock selloff worsened in Asia, with a regional benchmark dropping the most in more than a year, on concern the US will tighten regulations on the AI industry after Democrats’ decisive election win. European futures also headed lower. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is weighing whether to leave the Trump administration, people familiar with the matter said, as he considers his next moves following Republicans’ midterm elections wipeout this week. Rubio dismissed the report, telling the New York Times that he didn’t know where the information came from. Today's guests: Stéphane Boujnah, Euronext, CEO; Ellie Henderson, Investec, Economist. (Source: Bloomberg)

They also examine Apple's AI rollout in China and the privacy implications of new always-listening Apple Watch features. Have a question for Mark? Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.2% while those for the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.3%. Both fell earlier before buyers stepped in. The dollar weakened against major peers, while 10-year Treasury yields fell three basis points to 4.93%. Europe’s Stoxx 600 climbed 0.6% and a gauge for Asian equities was little changed. The Opening Trade has everything you need to know as markets open across Europe. With analysis you won't find anywhere else, we break down the biggest stories of the day and speak to top guests who have skin in the game. Hosted by Anna Edwards, Guy Johnson and Tom Mackenzie. item.title: An Election Day Special With Nate Silver
item.description:
Nate Silver tells us he is calling this midterms the “rock and a hard place election” — the background conditions are great for Democrats to win both the House and the Senate, but for that to come to pass, the party has to pull off some things that haven't happened in generations, like winning Texas. To believe that will happen requires a certain leap of faith, which is anathema to pollsters. Still, the polls generally believe Democrats are favored, but many professional pollsters would end up with egg on their face if the night does not go that way. Silver — the founder of Silver Bulletin — joins us today to discuss why popular narratives around polling error are wrong, prediction markets, why he doesn't think AI will replace pollsters, and what he is paying attention to tonight as the polls close. (Source: Bloomberg)

The structured products business in the US has gotten very large recently — on track to hit $300 billion in sales this year. What was once an opaque financial product is getting a lot more attention. So what are structured products, exactly, and how are they influencing the economy? In short, structured products are basically a fusion of a bank IOU with a derivative product, but that underplays how complex they are and how they are shaping market dynamics. On this episode, we speak with Alex Micalizzi, who is the international head of equity structured notes at Nomura, and he gives us what might be the clearest explanation of how structured products are created, how they work, and why sales in structured products has grown so much in the last year. item.title: Trump Can Drive Turnout on Both Sides: Taylor
item.description:
Jessica Taylor, Senate and Governors editor for The Cook Political Report, says President Donald Trump is needed on the campaign trail to drive Republican turnout, but making the midterms about himself could also motivate Democrats and independents to vote against his party. Taylor says Cook moved Florida's Senate race from Solid Republican to Likely Republican because it expects a single-digit contest and says Florida could offer an early indication of how Republicans are performing nationally. Taylor says some states could produce different results in their gubernatorial and Senate races and that the bigger question in the closing days is which voters ultimately turn out. She speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Killin Says Affordability Is Driving Colorado Race
item.description:
Jessica Killin, Colorado Democratic Congressional candidate, says affordability is the central concern she hears from voters and argues Congress needs to take back its power on tariffs and the war with Iran. Killin says tariffs are raising costs for small businesses and calls for Congress to play a larger role in pursuing a longer-term agreement with Iran while also addressing housing and health care. Killin says her Army and private-sector background gives her an understanding of how to help the economy grow and calls questions over her Colorado residency a nonissue after a judge dismissed the case. She speaks with Joe Mathieu and Kailey Leinz on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Intel, Amazon Earnings Spark Tech Selloff as AI Fears Mount
item.description:
Bloomberg Daybreak Europe is your essential morning viewing to stay ahead. Tech stocks sold off for a second consecutive day as a rotation out of the AI trade accelerated, after earnings from Amazon and Intel raised fresh concerns about capital expenditure. Binance has suffered the crypto industry’s biggest-ever hack in a fresh blow to efforts to push digital assets into the mainstream. The exchange said $6.3 billion worth of funds were affected, with $3 billion in crypto frozen, and that it had suspended all withdrawals as it works with law enforcement and completes a security revamp. And France unexpectedly contracted in the third quarter, putting the economy on a weak footing as it faces headwinds from surging borrowing costs, violent protests and political and budgetary uncertainty. Today guests: Gonzalo García San Miguel, Abenójar Tungsten, CEO; Sander van ’t Noordende, Randstad, CEO (Source: Bloomberg)
